summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base for network management, describing managed objects for Fibre Channel Registered State Change Notifications. It is a standards-track MIB module.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of dials and gauges that lets you watch the change notices on a storage network.

questions: snmp mib for fibre channel state change notifications
what is an rscn in fibre channel
how to monitor fibre channel rscn with snmp
subtitle: An SNMP MIB module for watching who is registered for Fibre Channel state change notices, and how many were sent or rejected.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel fabrics tell registered ports about changes through Registered State Change Notifications (RSCNs), but there was no standard SNMP way to see who is registered, count RSCNs or learn about rejected requests.
tldr.mechanism: The T11-FC-RSCN-MIB module defines a registration table, per-fabric statistics counters, and two SNMP notifications with control objects that report rejected SCR, RSCN and SW_RSCN requests.
tldr.outcome: Network management systems can monitor RSCN registrations and usage on Fibre Channel switches using SNMP, with the module registered under mib-2 as node 161.

today: RFC 4983 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the Fibre Channel Management MIB in RFC 4044.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 4983 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing Registered State Change Notifications (RSCNs) in a Fibre Channel network. It describes which Nx_Ports are registered to receive which types of RSCNs, the control and generation of SNMP notifications on registration failures, and RSCN-related statistics.

The memo was previously approved by INCITS Task Group T11.5, and this document is a product of the IETF's IMSS working group. It is written as an SMIv2 module, using the Internet-Standard Management Framework described in RFC 3410, RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a list of gauges for watching the change messages on a storage network, written in the standard way network gauges are described.

sections.title: Fibre Channel and RSCNs in Brief
sections.content:
Fibre Channel interconnects communication points called N_Ports, either through a switching network called a Fabric or by a point-to-point link. A port on a switch that faces an N_Port is an F_Port. On an Arbitrated Loop the switch port is an FL_Port and the node ports are NL_Ports. Nx_Port means either an N_Port or an NL_Port.

An Nx_Port can register with a State Change Registration (SCR) request to receive RSCNs. When an event may affect a registered port's state, it receives an RSCN. Examples given are failures of other nodes, new devices coming online, or more network-accessible storage becoming available. The payload gives the type of change and the address of the changed port. The sender may coalesce several events into one RSCN, and each RSCN is a request answered with an accept or reject.

A registered Nx_Port receives an RSCN as an Extended Link Service (ELS) request. Between switches, the Fabric distributes them in an SW_ILS frame carrying an SW_RSCN payload, which the switch converts into ELS requests for its registered ports. The RFC also notes that Virtual Fabrics, from FC-SW-4, tag each frame to say which Virtual Fabric it belongs to.
sections.plainLanguage: Some devices ask the switch, "tell me when anything changes." The switch then sends them a note whenever a device appears, disappears or changes.

sections.title: Indexes and Instances
sections.content:
Tables in the module are indexed so a manager can tell things apart. A Fibre Channel management instance, from RFC 4044, is a separable managed instance of Fibre Channel functionality, identified by fcmInstanceIndex. Each instance can manage one or more switches, identified by fcmSwitchIndex.

All Fabric-related information is indexed by an integer t11FcRscnFabricIndex, whose syntax comes from the T11-TC-MIB (RFC 4439). For a device on a single Physical Fabric without Virtual Fabrics, its value is always 1. With multiple Virtual or Physical Fabrics it distinguishes one fabric from another. When both appear in the same INDEX clause, fcmSwitchIndex is listed before the fabric index, which makes it simpler to query all fabrics a single switch connects to.

The module imports common textual conventions from RFC 4439 and the Name Server MIB (RFC 4438). It relates to the earlier Fibre Channel switch MIB (RFC 2837), which RFC 4044 replaced.
sections.plainLanguage: Each gauge has a label saying which switch and which network it belongs to, so nothing gets mixed up.

sections.title: The Four Object Groups
sections.content:
The module has four groups of objects.

  • Registration group. The table t11FcRscnRegTable lists Nx_Ports that registered to receive RSCNs, indexed by instance, switch, fabric and the registering port's address. The t11FcRscnRegType object is a BITS value: fromFabricController(0) for RSCNs about events the Fabric Controller detects, and fromNxPort(1) for events detected by the affected Nx_Port.
  • Statistics group. Counters at the message-type level for SCRs received and rejected, RSCNs sent, received and rejected, and SW_RSCNs sent, received and rejected. It also has in and out counters per RSCN Event Qualifier value.
  • Notify control group. One enable object for each notification, plus three objects recording the latest rejection: the content of the rejected request, its source, and the reason.
  • Notify group. Two notifications, one for a switch rejecting an SCR or RSCN and one for a switch rejecting an SW_RSCN.

Event Qualifier counters exist for 0000 (not specified), 0002 (changed port attribute), 0003 (changed service object), 0004 (changed switch configuration) and 0005 (removed object). There is none for 0001, changed name server object, because the Name Server MIB's t11NsInRscns and t11NsOutRscns already count it. A coalesced RSCN may be counted in more than one counter. The counters have no discontinuities other than those every Counter32 has when sysUpTime is 0.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a sign-up list, a set of counters, a few on and off switches, and two alarm bells for when a request is turned down.

sections.title: Notifications and Rejection Details
sections.content:
Two notifications exist. t11FcRscnElsRejectReqNotify is generated when a switch rejects an SCR or RSCN, and t11FcRscnIlsRejectReqNotify when it rejects an SW_RSCN. Each carries five objects: the rejected request string, its source, the reject reason code, the reason code explanation and the vendor-specific reason code.

The rejected request string is an octet string of 0 to 255 octets holding the payload in network byte order. It is the zero-length string if the payload is unavailable, and holds the first 255 octets if the payload is longer. The source is the WWN that sent the rejected request.

Two read-write objects, t11FcRscnIlsRejectNotifyEnable and t11FcRscnElsRejectNotifyEnable, switch each notification on or off. Both default to false, and values written SHOULD be retained over agent reboots.

The RFC explains why these notifications are not flow-controlled. Flow control is needed for data-plane events that could cause a chain reaction. Both notifications here come from control-plane events that cannot start one, so the extra complexity is not warranted.
sections.plainLanguage: When a switch says no to a sign-up or a message, it can ring a bell and write down who asked and why. You choose whether the bell is switched on.

sections.title: Compliance Requirements
sections.content: An implementation of the module must support the registration group, the notify control group and the notify group. The statistics group is mandatory only for systems that count such events. For the two notify enable objects, write access is not required, so read-only is acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: A switch has to keep the sign-up list and the alarm bells. Keeping score is only required if it already counts things.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The two notify enable objects are the only read-write objects the RFC lists as sensitive. If misconfigured they would generate unwanted notifications or suppress wanted ones. The registration, statistics and notify control tables are also listed as possibly sensitive to read.

The RFC notes that SNMP versions before SNMPv3 lacked adequate security. It is RECOMMENDED that implementors consider the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and deploying earlier SNMP versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must configure access so that only legitimate principals can GET or SET the objects.

For IANA, the RFC says an OID was assigned for the module under the appropriate subtree. The module identity is { mib-2 161 }.
sections.plainLanguage: The on and off switches should only be touched by the right people, and the lists should only be shown to people allowed to see them.
